Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Vignette:
During the summer of 2022, Kiet was working a routine service call at a commercial laundry facility on the outskirts of Portland, where a malfunctioning industrial dryer was leaking a solvent-based cleaning agent into the ventilation system. He had been an HVAC technician for twenty-three years and had walked into hundreds of mechanical rooms without a second thought. But that particular afternoon, within minutes of opening the access panel, his eyes began to sting, his throat tightened, and a wave of dizziness hit him so hard that he had to grip the metal railing to keep from collapsing. He stumbled outside, gasping, and sat on the loading dock for nearly an hour while his vision slowly cleared and his heart stopped hammering against his ribs. The paramedics who arrived told him he would be fine, that the exposure had been brief and the chemical levels were below the threshold for lasting harm, but Kiet could not shake the feeling that something inside him had been permanently altered. He went home that night and lay awake, listening to his own breathing, convinced that his lungs were filling with something invisible.

In the weeks that followed, Kiet began to notice that his body would not settle. Even when he was sitting on the couch after dinner, his shoulders stayed hunched, his jaw clenched, and his hands rested in tight fists on his knees. His wife, Malina, would touch his arm and ask if he was okay, and he would nod, but inside he was scanning the room—checking the windows, listening for unfamiliar sounds, cataloguing every possible source of danger. He started going through the house before bed, turning the locks on the front door and the sliding glass door twice, then three times, then four, until the click of the bolt felt certain. He knew, rationally, that the house was secure, that no one was coming, that the chemical leak had been contained and he had not been poisoned. But rational knowledge did not seem to reach the part of him that stayed vigilant. When Malina told him the house was safe, that the air quality test they had paid for came back clean, he heard the words but could not absorb them. Safety, for Kiet, had become a word that meant nothing unless he could verify it with his own hands.

The avoidance crept in slowly, almost without his noticing. He stopped accepting service calls at industrial sites, telling his dispatcher that he preferred residential work now, that he was getting too old for the heavy stuff. He began to dread the moments of quiet at home, when the television was off and the kids were asleep, because stillness felt like waiting for something bad to happen. He found himself filling every evening with tasks—organising the garage, cleaning the gutters, rewiring a lamp that did not need rewiring—anything to keep his mind occupied and his body moving. If he sat still for too long, the memory of that chemical burn in his throat would surface, and he would feel the dizziness again, even though he was standing perfectly steady. Relaxation had become a trap, a moment when the fear could catch up to him, and so he avoided it the way he avoided the loading dock at the laundry facility, the way he avoided being alone in the basement of his own house, the way he avoided any conversation that might turn toward what happened.

His marriage began to carry the weight of his vigilance. Malina would suggest a weekend away, and Kiet would feel his chest tighten at the thought of an unfamiliar hotel room, of not knowing the exits, of being somewhere he could not control. He told her he was too tired, that work had been busy, that maybe next month. She stopped asking after a while. At work, his colleagues noticed that he had become jumpy, that he flinched when someone walked up behind him, that he spent his lunch breaks in his truck with the doors locked rather than in the break room. He knew they were talking about him, but he could not bring himself to care. What mattered was staying alert, staying ready, staying safe—even if no one else understood why he could not believe he was safe.

It was a Wednesday evening in late October when Kiet finally called a clinic. He had been sitting in his truck in the driveway for twenty minutes, unable to open the door, because the house was dark and Malina was out with her sister, and the thought of walking into an empty building made his stomach turn. He sat there with the engine running, gripping the steering wheel, and realised that he could not keep living this way—checking, avoiding, tensing, waiting for a danger that never came but felt more real than anything else. He wanted to stop being afraid of his own home. He wanted to believe Malina when she said they were safe. He wanted to walk into a mechanical room without seeing that afternoon again. But most of all, he wanted to feel, just once, like his body belonged to him.
